title_zh: 为什么洗钱者偏爱 100 美元钞票：对话记者、作家 Oliver Bullough
subtitle_zh: 从现金悖论、贸易洗钱到轮播欺诈，揭开全球洗钱这门巨额生意的运作逻辑。

turns.en: Hello, Odd Lodge listeners. I'm Joe Wiesenthal.
turns.zh: Hello，Odd Lots 的听众们。我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: We're the hosts of the Odd Lodge podcast, and we've got something exciting for you.
turns.zh: 我们是 Odd Lots 播客的主持人，今天有个令人兴奋的消息要告诉大家。

turns.en: That's right. So one of the best parts of hosting our podcast is we get to actually meet and interact with our listeners. And we know we have some listeners over in Los Angeles.
turns.zh: 没错。主持这个播客最棒的一点，就是能真正跟我们的听众见面、互动。我们知道在 Los Angeles 就有一批听众。

turns.zh: 我们请来了几位非常令人期待的嘉宾，也安排了几场很棒的对话。所以赶紧去买票吧。你可以在 Bloomberg.com/oddlots 找到，或者点击节目备注下方的链接，到现场来跟我们打个招呼。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。播客。

turns.en: Radio. News. Music. Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Thoughts Podcast. I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 广播。新闻。音乐。Hello，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: Joe, everything I know about cash came from that tour we took of the Chicago Fed's cash facilities with its president, Austin Goolsbee.
turns.zh: Joe，我对现金的所有了解，都来自我们那次跟 Chicago Fed 主席 Austin Goolsbee 一起参观他们现金设施的经历。

turns.en: That was really fun. I'm trying to think. What do you remember? I remember just seeing lots and lots of cash, ink.
turns.zh: 那次真的很有意思。我在回想。你记得什么？我记得就是看到好多好多的现金、油墨。

turns.en: I remember appreciating the smell of the cash. It has a very idiosyncratic smell. smell. I remember the color of the cash, which you don't really notice all the different shades of dollar bills until you see them stacked up. Right.
turns.zh: 我记得我很欣赏现金的气味。它有一种非常独特的味道。我还记得现金的颜色，只有当你看到美元钞票堆成堆时，才会注意到它们其实有各种不同的色调。对吧。

turns.en: We just think of them as green.
turns.zh: 我们平时只觉得它们是绿色的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But there's like pinks in there and oranges. Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 但里面其实有粉色、有橙色。是的，确实如此。

turns.en: Fifty shades of green. And then one thing that I remember is Austin actually telling us that 85% of the $ 2. 4 trillion in circulation is happens to be $ 100 bills. Do you remember that? Yeah.
turns.zh: 绿色的五十种层次。然后我还记得 Austin 跟我们说，流通中那 2.4 万亿美元里，有 85% 恰好是 100 美元的钞票。你记得吗？记得。

turns.en: And this is one of those sort of like facts about the world that people seem to know, but don't really think through. It just sort of comes up every once in a while. This phenomenon that, you know, by and large, like two things I think people may know about the cash economy, which is by and large, people use less and less cash in their daily lives. That fact seems to have actually had no effect on the amount of cash in circulation.
turns.zh: 这算是那种人们好像知道、却没有真正深想过的关于世界的事实。它只是时不时冒出来一下。这个现象是——大体上，我觉得人们对现金经济可能知道两件事：一是大体上，人们在日常生活中用现金越来越少。而事实证明，这一点似乎对流通中的现金总量毫无影响。

turns.en: Right. It keeps growing.
turns.zh: 对。它还在不断增长。

turns.en: And then quite a bit of that cash in circulation is in relatively high denomination bills that are even used less than, say, the fives or the 20s.
turns.zh: 而且流通现金中相当大一部分是面额相对较高的钞票，它们的使用甚至比 5 美元、20 美元还少。

turns.en: Yeah, I don't know about you, but I do not walk around with a lot of $ 100 bills in my pocket.
turns.zh: 是啊，我不知道你怎样，反正我口袋里可不会揣着一大堆 100 美元的钞票到处走。

turns.en: No, me neither.
turns.zh: 不，我也不会。

turns.en: On the rare occasions when I do go to a cash machine, I always choose 20s or even fives and 10s, right? So the question is... What are people doing with all these $ 100 bills, right? And when we talked about it with Austin, he described it as a disconnect between the stats and the daily use of cash of most Americans. But I think there's kind of an obvious answer here, right? What are people doing with $ 100 bills?
turns.zh: 在少数几次我去 ATM 取钱的时候，我总是选 20 美元的，甚至 5 美元、10 美元的，对吧？所以问题就来了——人们拿这些 100 美元钞票到底在干什么？我们跟 Austin 聊这个时，他把它描述成统计数据与大多数美国人日常现金使用之间的一种脱节。但我觉得这里其实有个挺明显的答案，对吧？人们拿 100 美元钞票在做什么？

turns.en: Well, I have an answer because I can tell you the last time I walked around with a significant stack of $ 100 bills.
turns.zh: 嗯，我倒是有个答案，因为我可以告诉你，我上一次揣着一大叠 100 美元钞票到处走是什么时候。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: Okay. I was playing in a poker game in New York City, and it was not a regulated poker game, and I didn't lose all my money that night. And so I walked home with a lot of $ 100 bills. So maybe that is a sort of.
turns.zh: 好。当时我在 New York City 打一场扑克牌局，那不是受监管的牌局，而且那晚我没把钱输光。所以我就揣着一大堆 100 美元钞票走回家了。所以这也许算是某种。

turns.en: That's some good, humble bragging, Joe, about winning at poker.
turns.zh: Joe，你这可是在低调地炫耀自己打扑克赢了啊。

turns.en: I didn't win. I said I didn't lose all my money. But maybe that's sort of a clue about the types of activities that might lend themselves to high-denomination individual bills. Yes.
turns.zh: 我没赢。我说的是我没把钱输光。但也许这算是个线索，暗示哪类活动可能适合用大面额的单张钞票。是的。

turns.en: So this episode is- perhaps poker adjacent. We're going to be talking about money laundering, which we've never done an episode specifically devoted to money laundering. And it is in fact like a huge business.
turns.zh: 所以这一集——大概跟扑克沾点边。我们要聊的是洗钱（money laundering），我们从来没做过一期专门讲洗钱的节目。而它实际上是一门巨大的生意。

turns.en: Some of the numbers you read about them and they're like staggering. And I almost like don't believe some of the numbers, but when you figure out it's like, okay, drugs are probably a big deal. Fraud is probably a big deal. Crime is a big deal. People are trying to get their money out of countries that have various sort of rigid capital controls. China being an obvious example, you could see how it adds up.
turns.zh: 你读到的一些数字简直惊人。我几乎都不太相信其中一些数字，但当你想明白——好，毒品大概是个大买卖。欺诈大概是个大买卖。犯罪是个大买卖。还有人想把钱从那些有各种严格资本管制（capital controls）的国家转出去，China 就是个明显的例子——你就能看出这些是怎么累加起来的。

turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And of course, money laundering is kind of the thing that makes a lot of crime possible, right? Like a lot of people wouldn't be in the crime business if they couldn't actually use the money they're generating from it and money laundering. is the way they're able to do that. So I think it's a worthy subject to dive into.
turns.zh: 是啊，完全没错。而且当然，洗钱正是让很多犯罪得以实现的东西，对吧？很多人如果没法真正花掉他们从犯罪中赚来的钱，就不会干这行；而洗钱就是他们能做到这一点的方式。所以我觉得这是个值得深入探讨的话题。

turns.en: I really want to learn more about how it all works.
turns.zh: 我真的很想多了解一下这一切是怎么运作的。

turns.en: All right, let's do it. We do, in fact, have the perfect guest. We're going to be speaking with Oliver Bullough. He is a journalist and author of Everybody Loves Our Dollars. So Oliver, thanks so much for coming on All Thoughts.
turns.zh: 好，我们开始吧。我们确实请到了最合适的嘉宾。我们将对话 Oliver Bullough。他是一位记者，也是 Everybody Loves Our Dollars 一书的作者。Oliver，非常感谢你来上 Odd Lots。

turns.en: And thanks for having me on the show. I'm really pleased to be here.
turns.zh: 也谢谢你们邀请我上节目。我非常高兴能来这里。

turns.en: Talk to us about the scale of money laundering, because you sometimes hear these statistics thrown out, like bigger than the entire GDP of Germany, certainly bigger than a lot of big tech companies and things like that. How large are we talking about here?
turns.zh: 跟我们说说洗钱的规模吧，因为你有时会听到有人抛出这些统计数据，比如比 Germany 的整个 GDP 还大，肯定比很多大型科技公司还大之类的。我们说的到底有多大？

turns.en: Well, it's worth saying in advance that obviously no one really knows. The criminals are not filing accurate tax returns. So there's a lot of supposition going on here. But the most widely used estimate is that We're talking about between 2% and 5% of global GDP. And since global GDP is approximately $ 100 trillion, that means between $ 2 and $ 5 trillion being laundered globally. And that's a pretty decent amount of money. You could build quite a lot of data centers with that. And that's growing all the time.
turns.zh: 嗯，有必要先说明，显然没有人真正知道确切数字。罪犯可不会如实报税。所以这里面有很多推测。但最广泛使用的估计是，我们说的是全球 GDP 的 2% 到 5% 之间。而由于全球 GDP 大约是 100 万亿美元，这意味着全球被洗的钱在 2 万亿到 5 万亿美元之间。这可是相当大一笔钱。用这些钱你能建相当多的数据中心（data centers）。而且这个规模还在不断增长。

turns.en: I like how we measure everything in data centers now. How many data centers can you build?
turns.zh: 我喜欢现在我们都用数据中心来衡量一切。你能建多少个数据中心？

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, I mean, I don't know if the criminals are building a lot of data centers. I mean, they are choosing almost any avenue they can find to launder their money. So perhaps that's the new new thing. But the old things are still very much current. We're talking about, obviously, cash money earlier. And although we like to focus on shiny things, crypto for laundering money, I mean, criminals are pretty traditional in a lot of the ways they move their cash. So we are often talking about literal banknotes.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，我不知道罪犯是不是在建很多数据中心。他们几乎会选任何能找到的渠道来洗钱。所以也许那是最新的新玩法。但老办法依然非常流行。我们前面显然谈到了现金。尽管我们喜欢盯着那些光鲜的东西，比如用加密货币（crypto）洗钱，但罪犯在转移现金的很多方式上其实相当传统。所以我们经常说的就是实实在在的钞票。

turns.en: Do you have a sense of how that 2% to 5% number is derived? Because yes, we've seen that stat, et cetera. But also, as you've said, no one is filing these things in any sort of official manner. It's a lot of money. Do you have a sense of why people think it's in that ballpark?
turns.zh: 你了解这个 2% 到 5% 的数字是怎么得出来的吗？因为，是的，我们见过这个统计数据之类的。但正如你所说，也没有任何人以任何官方方式申报这些东西。这是很大一笔钱。你大概知道为什么人们认为它就在那个区间吗？

turns.en: That's a really good question, actually. It derives from an estimate given by Michel Candesso, who was the head of the International Monetary Fund back in the late 90s, a French central banker. And he came up with this idea in the late 90s that it was between 2% and 5% of global GDP, which was based on a couple of economists' work at the time trying to work out the size of the global economy. And it was very much a guesstimate at the time. And it's been attacked from lots of different directions, trying to work it out in a sort of a macro way, looking at it in micro way, trying to work at various dimensions. guesses. And people do keep coming back to this kind of a range. So the estimate that tends to be given is two to five percent. It's the same estimate that was given in the late 90s, which is it's a kind of uncomfortable truth hidden in that estimate, which is that if the scale or the share of the global economy that is criminal is the same now as it was in the 1990s, it means that everything we've done to try and tackle money laundering, which has been an failed to do anything except perhaps prevent the criminal economy from getting bigger. Criminals have been able to outmanoeuvre regulators and law enforcement agencies and governments' attempts to limit them by a sort of ceaseless entrepreneurial nature ever since there have been attempts to stop them from laundering money. And the fact that their share of the global economy just grows alongside the global economy is proof of that.
turns.zh: 这其实是个非常好的问题。它源自 Michel Candesso 给出的一个估计，他是 90 年代末 International Monetary Fund 的负责人，一位 French 央行官员。他在 90 年代末提出了这个说法，即洗钱规模在全球 GDP 的 2% 到 5% 之间，这是基于当时几位经济学家试图测算全球经济规模的工作。在当时，这非常像一个连蒙带猜的估计（guesstimate）。它从很多不同方向受到过质疑，人们试着从宏观角度去测算，从微观角度去看，试图从各个维度去推算。种种猜测。而人们确实不断回到这样一个区间。所以通常给出的估计就是 2% 到 5%。这跟 90 年代末给出的估计是一样的，而这个估计里藏着一个令人不太舒服的真相：如果全球经济中属于犯罪部分的规模或占比，现在跟 1990 年代一样，那就意味着我们为打击洗钱所做的一切——除了也许阻止了犯罪经济变得更大之外，什么都没做成。自从有人试图阻止罪犯洗钱以来，罪犯凭借一种永不停歇的创业精神，一直能够绕开监管者、执法机构以及各国政府的限制。而他们占全球经济的份额只是随着全球经济一同增长，这一点就是明证。

turns.en: Yeah. The fact that it's growing in tandem with like broader economic growth. Absolutely. So, okay, what's going on with our efforts to actually tackle money laundering? Because I used to cover the banking industry. And one thing you would hear from banks all the time is how onerous KYC regulation, know your customer regulation was, how terrible it was that they had to file thousands and thousands of like suspicious activity reports, lots and lots of complaints about everything they're doing to stamp out suspicious or illegal activity. But at the same time, per your commentary, it doesn't seem like it's actually been effective.
turns.zh: 是啊。它跟更广泛的经济增长同步增长这一点。完全没错。那好，我们真正打击洗钱的努力现在是什么情况？因为我以前报道过银行业。你从银行那里经常听到的一件事，就是 KYC 监管、也就是了解你的客户（know your customer）监管有多么繁重，他们不得不提交成千上万份可疑活动报告（suspicious activity reports）有多糟糕，还有大量关于他们为消除可疑或非法活动所做一切的抱怨。但与此同时，按你的说法，这些努力似乎并没有真正见效。

turns.en: It's obviously easy to dismiss what banks say as special pleading, but actually they do have a point. We have an incredibly intrusive and onerous system put in place to try and stop money laundering and terrorist financing, which was, I mean, it was created the first AML legislation. The sort of rather weirdly named Bank Secrecy Act was passed back in 1970 in the US, and then it spread in globally when it became clear that one country couldn't fight money laundering on its own, because it was pretty easy to just fly your banknotes to the Bahamas, Cayman Islands or Panama. And then, so it's pretty important to have their cooperation and then everyone had to cooperate. So we ended up from the late 80s, thanks to an institution called the Financial Action Task Force with a kind of global approach to tackling money laundering, which has become incredibly intrusive, incredibly expensive. The estimates from LexisNexis is that global compliance with AML legislation, it costs something like $ 200 billion a year, which is a lot of money. I mean, if you look at what you could do with that money if you weren't using it for this, that would be enough to solve world hunger and to provide clean water and sanitation to everyone on Earth with about $ 50 billion left over. So it's a huge amount of money which is being spent on this issue. And a lot of that money is being spent by banks who are expected to check transactions to use ever more elaborate AI-powered compliance software, which they are doing. They are attempting to do the job being asked of them. They face very large fines if they don't do that job. So it's fairly easy to see why they're doing it, but it's not working. The system that we have is incredibly laborious, very bureaucratic. It generates, as you say, millions upon millions of suspicious activity reports every year, but it is signally failing to stop the money launderers who are always at least one step ahead.
turns.zh: 把银行的说法当作自我开脱而一笑置之，显然很容易，但他们其实说得有道理。我们建立了一套极其侵扰、极其繁重的制度，试图阻止洗钱和恐怖主义融资。也就是说，第一部反洗钱（AML）立法——名字相当古怪的 Bank Secrecy Act——早在 1970 年就在 US 通过了，随后当人们意识到一个国家没法独自打击洗钱时，它就传遍了全球，因为把钞票直接飞到 Bahamas、Cayman Islands 或 Panama 实在太容易了。所以，取得它们的配合就非常重要，然后所有人都得配合。于是从 80 年代末开始，多亏了一个叫 Financial Action Task Force 的机构，我们有了一种打击洗钱的全球性方法，而它已经变得极其侵扰、极其昂贵。LexisNexis 的估计是，全球遵守 AML 立法的成本大约每年 2000 亿美元，这是很大一笔钱。我是说，如果你看看这笔钱要是不花在这上面能做什么——它足以解决世界饥饿问题，为地球上每个人提供清洁饮水和卫生设施，还能剩下大约 500 亿美元。所以在这个问题上花的钱是巨量的。而其中很多钱是银行花的，它们被要求核查交易、使用越来越精密的 AI 驱动合规软件，它们确实在这么做。它们在努力完成被要求做的工作。如果做不到，就会面临巨额罚款。所以它们为什么这么做很容易理解，但这套做法并不奏效。我们现有的制度极其费力、非常官僚化。正如你所说，它每年产生数以百万计的可疑活动报告，却明显没能阻止那些洗钱者——他们总是至少领先一步。

turns.en: So obviously, we really want to get into the details of the creative ways that criminals and so forth move money across borders. But just to sort of set the scene a little bit, we started this conversation by talking about how much cash there is in circulation and the prevalence of high denomination bills. We're also talking about all the suspicious sort of incident reports that banks file. Big picture, I sort of have two questions. One is, what is the general sense of the distribution? How much is this happening via cash and bearer instruments that are hard to track? And how much, you know, we see the headlines from time to time, a bank will get into really big trouble. HSBC got into trouble years ago. How much do we think is happening sort of inside regulated financial institutions that didn't identify the illegal movement of money?
turns.zh: 所以显然，我们非常想深入了解罪犯之流跨境转移资金的那些富有创意的手法的细节。但先稍微铺垫一下背景：我们这段对话是从流通中有多少现金、以及大面额钞票有多普遍谈起。我们还谈到了银行提交的所有那些可疑事件报告。从大局看，我大概有两个问题。一是，总体上分布是怎样的？其中有多少是通过现金和难以追踪的无记名票据（bearer instruments）进行的？又有多少——你知道，我们时不时会看到头条新闻，某家银行摊上大麻烦，HSBC 多年前就出过事——有多少是发生在受监管的金融机构内部、这些机构没能识别出资金的非法流动？

turns.en: Obviously, it is happening via regulated financial institutions. We know this because occasionally they get caught, whether that's Danske Bank or Deutsche Bank, HSBC, whoever. But if you look at the scale of global cash smuggling, and you compare that to the amounts that are even in these gigantic money laundering scams, which are accused of going through regulated financial institutions, it's just an absolutely different league. Danske Bank was accused of moving, if I remember rightly, about 130 billion over several years for suspicious Russian clients. Global cash smuggling is certainly in the hundreds of billions annually. Cash is a hugely significant tool for moving illicit wealth around the world. And even that is dwarfed by what we refer to as trade-based money laundering. It is essentially a way of moving value around the world, not in the form of money at all, but in the form of stuff. If you are moving value out of China, it's far easier to do it in the form of essentially misinvoicing a shipment of manufactured goods or knock off designer clothes or whatever than it is to move it in the form of money at all. So there is a focus on the regulated sector, banks in particular, when we talk about money laundering for obvious reasons, because it's sort of easy to look in a spreadsheet and see value moving around. But actually, it's a far bigger deal if you look at how money is moved in the form of cash and how money is moved in the form of stuff. And that form of money laundering, trade-based money laundering, is almost impossible to estimate. I mean, there is an institution in Washington, Global Financial Integrity, that estimates that that's about a trillion dollars a year is moved via trade-based money laundering. You know, we're talking about amounts of money being laundered outside the financial system that completely dwarfs what's happening within the financial system.
turns.zh: 显然，它是通过受监管的金融机构发生的。我们知道这一点，是因为它们偶尔会被抓个正着，不管是 Danske Bank、Deutsche Bank、HSBC 还是谁。但如果你看看全球现金走私的规模，再把它跟那些被指控经由受监管金融机构进行的、即便是巨型洗钱骗局里的金额相比，那完全就是另一个量级。我记得没错的话，Danske Bank 被指控在数年间为一些可疑的 Russian 客户转移了大约 1300 亿。而全球现金走私每年肯定在数千亿美元级别。现金是围绕全球转移非法财富的一种极其重要的工具。而即便是这个规模，跟我们所说的基于贸易的洗钱（trade-based money laundering）相比也相形见绌。它本质上是一种在全球转移价值的方式，完全不是以货币的形式，而是以货物的形式。如果你要把价值转出 China，那么本质上通过对一批制成品、山寨名牌服装之类的货物做虚假开票（misinvoicing）来转移，要比以货币形式转移容易得多。所以谈到洗钱时，出于显而易见的原因，重点会放在受监管的部门、尤其是银行上，因为在一张电子表格里看到价值流动是比较容易的。但实际上，如果你看看资金如何以现金形式转移、如何以货物形式转移，那才是大得多的问题。而那种形式的洗钱，也就是基于贸易的洗钱，几乎无法估算。我是说，Washington 有个机构叫 Global Financial Integrity，它估计每年通过基于贸易的洗钱转移的资金大约有一万亿美元。你知道，我们说的是在金融体系之外被洗掉的资金量，它完全让金融体系内部发生的事情相形见绌。

turns.en: Yeah, so one thing I learned from your book is there's a connection between drug money and I guess John Deere tractors and other equipment with the Mexican cartels, like essentially trading fentanyl for farming equipment. Can you walk us through that particular example? How does this actually work?
turns.zh: 是啊，我从你的书里学到的一件事是，毒资跟——我想是 John Deere 拖拉机和其他设备——与 Mexican 贩毒集团之间存在关联，本质上是拿芬太尼（fentanyl）换农业设备。你能带我们梳理一下这个具体的例子吗？这实际上是怎么运作的？

turns.en: Well, you can see this. It's just logical that if there is, let's say, $ 50 billion worth of cocaine arriving in the United States every year, I've just invented that number, but it's a nice round number. So let's say it is that. then there must be $ 50 billion of something else flowing in the opposite direction for the books of the cartels to balance. They're not in this for charitable reasons. They like to make a living out of moving drugs, so that follows. Now, obviously, a significant amount of that is in the form of money. By best estimates, something like $ 25 billion worth of cash is smuggled into Mexico every year. But there's still a significant hole in the books that needs to be filled with something. And it has been a traditional practice that essentially a way of meeting that hole in the books is just by exporting stuff. What does America make particularly well? Well, I mean, Caterpillar tractors, John Deere tractors, that's useful. Everyone wants those. You can send them south. You can send all kinds of wonderful American financial products. We see this in Europe to a greater degree with luxury goods. There is a huge demand in China for European luxury goods, whether that's Gucci handbags or Burberry anorex or whatever. And so there is a giant off the books, a sort of grey market, of designer goods which flow out of Europe into China. And in return, we receive criminal goods or drugs in return. So essentially anything that is being made well in one place, whether that's Caterpillar tractors or Gucci handbags, can just be as useful a form of money as anything else. I mean, you need to just think about criminals as being endlessly looking for ways of finding concentrated value in a way that isn't going to be checked so they can move it around. Obviously, the most Useful example of that at all would be an expensive watch. If you buy a million dollar watch, you can fly in from one country to another and sell it at the other end. No one's going to check it when you fly across the world, sell it at the other end, and you've just moved a million dollars without having to move a million dollars. It's as simple as that. And it happens all the time, absolutely everywhere.
turns.zh: 嗯，你能看出来。这在逻辑上很自然：如果比如说每年有价值 500 亿美元的可卡因（cocaine）运抵 United States——这个数字是我随口编的，但它是个不错的整数。就假设是这个数——那么为了让贩毒集团的账目平衡，就必须有价值 500 亿美元的其他东西朝相反方向流动。他们干这个不是为了做慈善。他们喜欢靠贩毒谋生，所以这是顺理成章的。当然，其中很大一部分是以货币形式。按最好的估计，每年大约有 250 亿美元的现金被走私进 Mexico。但账上仍然有一个相当大的窟窿需要用别的东西来填补。而一种传统做法，本质上就是通过出口货物来填补账上这个窟窿。America 特别擅长制造什么？嗯，我是说，Caterpillar 拖拉机、John Deere 拖拉机，这些很有用。人人都想要。你可以把它们往南送。你还可以送各种各样出色的 American 金融产品。在 Europe，我们在更大程度上能看到这一点，是用奢侈品。China 对 European 奢侈品有巨大需求，不管是 Gucci 手袋、Burberry 什么什么的。于是就有了一个庞大的、账外的、某种灰色市场（grey market）的名牌商品，从 Europe 流向 China。作为回报，我们收到犯罪货物或毒品。所以本质上，任何在一个地方被制造得很好的东西，不管是 Caterpillar 拖拉机还是 Gucci 手袋，都可以像其他任何东西一样，成为一种有用的货币形式。我是说，你只需要把罪犯理解成在无止境地寻找方法，找到一种不会被核查的、浓缩的价值，好让它能四处转移。显然，这方面最有用的例子就是一块昂贵的手表。如果你买一块价值一百万美元的手表，你可以从一个国家飞到另一个国家，然后在另一端把它卖掉。当你飞越全球时没人会检查它，在另一端卖掉，你就刚刚转移了一百万美元，而无需真的去转移一百万美元现金。就这么简单。而且这种事无时无刻不在发生，绝对无处不在。

turns.en: It is kind of crazy that you have to declare like more than $ 10, 000 in cash at the airport, but you could easily have a $ 1 million watch on your wrist.
turns.zh: 有点疯狂的是，你在机场必须申报超过 1 万美元的现金，但你却可以轻轻松松戴着一块价值 100 万美元的手表在手腕上。

turns.en: No one would think anything of that. Talk to us a little bit more about, all right, so Tracy asked about the Mexican trade of cocaine for tractors, which sounds reasonable enough. Talk to us about how money is moved out of China, the popular ways to move money out of China at scale. You mentioned sort of watch and handbags, but what is the shape of this trade?
turns.zh: 没人会对此多想。再多跟我们讲讲——好，Tracy 问了关于 Mexico 用可卡因换拖拉机的交易，那听起来还算合理。跟我们说说资金是如何被移出 China 的，那些大规模把钱转出 China 的流行方式。你提到了手表和手袋之类的，但这门交易到底是什么形态？

turns.en: The basis of the trade is that there is a restriction on moving money out of China of $ 50, 000 per person per year. Now, $ 50, 000 might sound like quite a lot to the average Chinese person, but to a wealthy Chinese person, that's not nearly enough. So there is a constant demand from wealthy Chinese people outside China for money that they can't move in a formal way. And so there is a huge appetite, a huge demand for cash, for some form of money. And now what they really need is a supply of money, which they can meet in coming in the opposite direction. And then brokers can put those two together. And fortunately, in the West, we have created that supply of money by making drugs illegal. So there is a gigantic supply of cash, which is being generated in an illegal way. And the Chinese money laundering networks, which have become incredibly sophisticated in the last, particularly the last 15 years, last 10 years, all over the world, essentially have created a business model of putting together this demand for cash that comes from wealthy Chinese people outside China and the supply of cash that comes from the cartels or other drugs gangs in Europe. It's often the Albanians or the Andrangheta in Italy and in In the US, obviously, it'd be more than the Mexicans or the Colombians. And they put these two together, the Chinese demand and the cartel supply. This is often called the Vancouver model, slightly unfairly, because it doesn't only happen in Vancouver. But it was first identified in Vancouver, where you would get this totally baffled police officers watching this phenomenon of wealthy Chinese people being given carrier bags full of banknotes outside casinos, going into the casinos, and then just losing all the money. Because laundering money via casinos is something that's been happening ever since the mob took over Las Vegas. It's a super easy way of laundering money. You bet a little bit, you cash in your chips, then you sell the chips and you just have clean money. And so that's very tightly controlled, but they couldn't really understand what was happening because that wasn't what was happening in Vancouver. They were just taking in money and then losing it. But if you zoomed out, you would see that this one transaction of handing over the cash to a Chinese gambler was just a small fraction of what was really happening in that you had a debt being created essentially. from the Chinese gambler to the drugs gang, which would be being repaid by supplying drugs to the drugs gang that they were able to sell to generate more cash, to hand it over to generate more gambling. And so you end up with essentially a circular transaction where money would change hand in China between a criminal gang and a wealthy Chinese person. Money would change hands in Canada between a drugs gang giving it to a Chinese person. And then essentially that would all net out by the movement of drugs between borders, which is how the value actually transfers. And you see this now. I mean, that's only like a bilateral trade, as it were, between Vancouver and China. But you see this now globally. So it might be the movement of luxury goods from Europe, the UK or France to China, then the movement of some kind of illicit goods or even totally normal goods from China to South America, then the movement of cocaine from South America to Europe, which would essentially complete this triangular trade. This happens globally on a truly colossal scale. And this is essentially how money is moved. You don't need to move money internationally, because that's where the checks are on transactions. You just move value internationally in the form of luxury goods, cocaine, or illicit goods of whatever kind. And so essentially, wherever you get criminality, there is a demand for money laundering, because this is how you realise... and protect your criminal profits. And this essentially is a gigantic parallel financial system. And what I find particularly pleasing about this, of looking at this, is this is pleasing is maybe not the word, but I'm kind of a nerd.
turns.zh: 这门交易的基础是，China 对把钱转出境有一个限制，即每人每年 5 万美元。对普通 Chinese 人来说，5 万美元也许听起来相当多，但对一个富有的 Chinese 人来说，那远远不够。所以在中国境外的富裕 Chinese 人当中，一直存在着对他们无法以正规方式转移的资金的需求。于是就有了对现金、对某种形式货币的巨大渴望、巨大需求。而他们现在真正需要的，是一个反向迎面而来的资金供给。然后中介（brokers）就能把这两者撮合到一起。而幸运的是，在西方，我们通过把毒品定为非法，制造出了那份资金供给。所以有了一个以非法方式产生的、巨量的现金供给。而那些 Chinese 洗钱网络——尤其在过去 15 年、过去 10 年里，在世界各地变得极其老练——本质上创造了一种商业模式，把来自中国境外富裕 Chinese 人的现金需求，与来自 Europe 的贩毒集团或其他毒品帮派（在 Italy 常常是 Albanians 或 'Ndrangheta，而在 US 显然更多是 Mexicans 或 Colombians）的现金供给撮合到一起。他们把这两者对接起来：Chinese 需求和贩毒集团供给。这常被称为 Vancouver model（温哥华模式），这个说法稍显不公，因为它并非只发生在 Vancouver。但它最早是在 Vancouver 被识别出来的，在那里你会看到完全一头雾水的警察，目睹这样一种现象：富有的 Chinese 人在赌场外被人递上装满钞票的购物袋，走进赌场，然后把钱全输光。因为通过赌场洗钱，自从黑帮接管 Las Vegas 以来就一直在发生。这是一种超级容易的洗钱方式。你稍微下点注，把筹码兑现，然后卖掉筹码，你就有了干净的钱。所以那被管得很严，但警察实在搞不懂发生了什么，因为在 Vancouver 发生的并不是那种情况。他们只是把钱拿进去、然后输掉。但如果你把镜头拉远，你会看到，把现金交给一个 Chinese 赌客的这一笔交易，只是真正发生的事情中的一小部分：本质上你产生了一笔债务，从 Chinese 赌客欠向毒品帮派，而这笔债务会通过向毒品帮派供货毒品来偿还，那些毒品他们能卖掉以产生更多现金，再把现金交出去以产生更多赌博。于是你最终得到一个本质上的循环交易：钱在 China 境内于一个犯罪团伙和一个富裕 Chinese 人之间易手；钱在 Canada 境内于一个毒品帮派把它交给一个 Chinese 人时易手；然后本质上，这一切都通过毒品跨境流动而相互抵消净额，而这才是价值实际转移的方式。你现在能看到这种模式。我是说，那还只是 Vancouver 和 China 之间的一种双边交易，可以这么说。但现在你在全球都能看到。所以它可能是奢侈品从 Europe、UK 或 France 流向 China，然后某种非法货物、甚至完全正常的货物从 China 流向 South America，再然后可卡因从 South America 流向 Europe，这基本上就完成了这个三角贸易。这在全球以真正庞大的规模发生。而这本质上就是资金被转移的方式。你不需要在国际间转移货币，因为那正是对交易进行核查的地方。你只需以奢侈品、可卡因或任何种类非法货物的形式，在国际间转移价值。所以本质上，凡是有犯罪的地方，就有对洗钱的需求，因为这就是你实现……并保护你的犯罪利润的方式。而这本质上是一个庞大的平行金融体系。而我觉得这一点特别有意思——'有意思'也许不是恰当的词，但我算是个书呆子。

turns.en: Intellectually satisfying.
turns.zh: 智识上的满足。

turns.en: Intellectually satisfying. This is exactly how the Medici's used to bank in the late medieval, early Renaissance Florence, is that they were moving wealth. They had an incredibly sophisticated system whereby you could deposit money at a branch of their bank in Venice or Florence, and then you could collect that same money in Bruges or in London and the other side of the Alps and the other end of Europe. Essentially, as soon as you could get there, the money was available for you to pick up. And, how did they move the money? They obviously weren't moving bullion from Italy to Belgium or Italy to the UK for the same reason that ordinary people would want to do that. It wasn't safe. So they were just moving trade. So silk going north or spices, wool coming south. And then we're just hiding the movement of cash in the paperwork. And, you know, in the years after World War II, some academics found their, what they were called their secret books in the state archive in Florence, and you could see how they were doing this. Essentially, they were providing banking services to politicians, to leading cardinals, other people in the church, in exactly the same way that banks might provide secret services now to politicians or any powerful people. And we're just hiding the transactions in the huge amount of paperwork generated by their trading activity. And this is basically now what the Chinese money laundering networks do. And you can tell that they're important. This is one of these weird things in money laundering studies, which is a very niche area, which is mainly just consists of me and about three other guys. But the money laundering studies, it is infested with acronyms, AML, anti-money laundering, CFT, counterfinance of terrorism. But if it's a really important one, it's a four-letter acronym, not a three-letter one. So the fact that Chinese money laundering networks are CMLNs, it's a four-letter acronym. You know that that's a big deal.
turns.zh: 智识上的满足。这恰恰就是 Medici 家族在中世纪晚期、文艺复兴早期的 Florence 做银行业务的方式，也就是他们在转移财富。他们有一套极其精密的系统，你可以在他们银行位于 Venice 或 Florence 的分行存钱，然后在 Bruges 或 London——阿尔卑斯山的另一边、Europe 的另一头——取出同一笔钱。基本上，只要你能到达那里，钱就在那里等你提取。那么，他们是怎么转移这笔钱的？他们显然不会把金银条块从 Italy 运到 Belgium、或从 Italy 运到 UK，理由跟普通人想做这件事时一样：不安全。所以他们只是转移贸易。于是丝绸往北走，香料、羊毛往南走。然后他们只是把现金的流动藏在这些单据文书里。你知道，在 World War II 之后的那些年，一些学者在 Florence 的国家档案馆里找到了他们的——所谓他们的'秘密账本'，你能看出他们是怎么做这件事的。本质上，他们在为政客、为主要枢机主教（cardinals）、为教会里的其他人提供银行服务，方式跟如今银行可能为政客或任何有权势的人提供隐秘服务一模一样。而他们只是把这些交易藏在贸易活动所产生的海量文书里。而这基本上就是现在 Chinese 洗钱网络所做的事。而且你能看出它们很重要。这是洗钱研究（money laundering studies）里一个奇怪的特点——这是个非常小众的领域，基本上就只有我和另外大约三个家伙在做。但洗钱研究里到处都是缩写词，AML（反洗钱）、CFT（反恐融资，counterfinance of terrorism）。但如果是个真正重要的缩写，它会是四个字母，而不是三个。所以 Chinese 洗钱网络是 CMLNs——一个四字母缩写，这就说明它是件大事。

turns.en: There does seem to be something very traditionalist about, I guess, trade-based money laundering. But on a related note, can you talk to us about the carousel fraud that was taking place going in and out of the UK? And then when the rules were finally changed, I think it just shifted over to Europe, which kind of gets at the point that it seems very hard to fix what is like a jurisdictional arbitrage issue unless you have some sort of harmonization across different countries.
turns.zh: 基于贸易的洗钱，确实似乎有一种非常传统的东西。但在一个相关的话题上，你能跟我们说说进出 UK 的那场轮播欺诈（carousel fraud）吗？后来规则终于被改了，我想它就转移到了 Europe，这多少触及了那个要点：似乎很难修复这种司法管辖套利（jurisdictional arbitrage）问题，除非你在不同国家之间有某种协调统一。

turns.en: Yeah, the carousel fraud is one of these absolutely fascinating crimes, which it's so complicated and so extraordinary that you think that if the criminals had designed it, if instead that they decided to set themselves to solving climate change or anything, then that problem would be solved. The kind of elaborate nature of the transactions they were doing, it grows out of a flaw in the way that the value added tax is designed in the European Union. Back then the UK was in the European Union. And essentially, the way it works is that if you're moving money, goods within a country, you charge value added tax. But if you move it between countries, you don't. So that difference had to be that way, because otherwise you would end up with the UK tax authority having to trust the French tax authority. And that's obviously never going to happen. So you had to have that zero rated transaction across borders, which just meant that you could cycle things in and out of one country and another country. and essentially claim VAT that you'd never actually paid. And it went round and round and round. And that's why it's called carousel fraud. It went round like a merry-go-round. And it started off as just this very simple transactions. And then as the tax authorities picked up on that, they became more and more complicated with different chains of shell companies going in all directions and incredibly complicated. But yeah, like you say, what's really interesting about it is the UK actually got very good at tackling this. And I actually use it in the book as an example of how to fight financial crime. It was a really fully multi-agency approach, like not just leaving it to the banks like we do with money laundering, but really fighting it with everything that the state had. And actually got very good at tackling this, but it just crossed into the rest of Europe, where now it's a 50 billion euro a year problem, carousel fraud. And it's so elaborate and so well-developed that you're talking about something that spreads from Lithuania down to Portugal, from Greece to Sweden.
turns.zh: 是啊，轮播欺诈是那种绝对令人着迷的犯罪之一，它如此复杂、如此非同寻常，以至于你会想，如果罪犯当初把这份心思——不去设计这套骗局，而是决定去解决气候变化或别的什么问题，那问题早就被解决了。他们所做交易的这种精密性质，源自 European Union 增值税（value added tax，VAT）设计方式上的一个漏洞。当时 UK 还在 European Union 里。基本上，它的运作方式是：如果你在一个国家内部转移货物，你要收增值税；但如果你在国家之间转移，就不收。这个差异必须是这样的，因为否则你就会落得 UK 税务当局不得不信任 French 税务当局的局面。而那显然永远不会发生。所以你必须让跨境交易零税率（zero rated），这就意味着你可以让货物在一个国家和另一个国家之间循环进出，本质上申领你其实从未真正缴过的增值税。它一圈又一圈地转。这就是为什么它叫轮播欺诈。它像旋转木马一样转圈。它一开始只是这种非常简单的交易。后来随着税务当局察觉到，它变得越来越复杂，有不同链条的空壳公司（shell companies）朝各个方向延伸，极其复杂。但是的，就像你说的，真正有意思的是，UK 其实变得非常擅长打击它。我在书里还把它当作如何打击金融犯罪的一个例子。那是一种真正完全的多机构协作方式，不像我们对洗钱那样只把它甩给银行，而是用国家所拥有的一切手段去真正打击它。而且确实变得非常擅长打击它，但它就转移到了 Europe 的其他地方，如今在那里它成了每年 500 亿欧元的问题——轮播欺诈。它是如此精密、如此发达，以至于你谈论的这个东西从 Lithuania 一直蔓延到 Portugal，从 Greece 到 Sweden。

turns.en: Can you explain the mechanics? I get that it's elaborate. But for the listeners, what is the mechanism?
turns.zh: 你能解释一下其中的机制吗？我懂它很精密。但对听众来说，这个机制到底是什么？

turns.en: This may be stretching the tolerance even of the odd lots to really explain. So it's called carousel fraud or missing trader intercommunity fraud, MTIC, which is a four letter acronym. So you can tell it's a big deal. But basically what you have is if you import a product, let's say from Ireland, if you're in the UK, and then you don't pay VAT on that trade because you've imported it, right? So no taxes paid. you then sell it to another shell company, which is controlled by you, but it looks like a different company in the UK. You charge VAT on that trade. So you add 20% or whatever the percentage is of VAT on that trade. And then you export the good back to Ireland. Now, if the second company exports the good, because they've exported it, they can claim from the treasury, they can claim the 20% back again. They can claim that 20% because that's what they get because they've exported the good. So essentially you export it, but without ever having paid paid it in the first place, you're essentially claiming back VAT that you never paid. So it's called missing trader intercommunity fraud because the trader that is supposed to pay the VAT to the treasury just vanishes. They go missing and they never pay it. So you are claiming back a tax that has never been paid, which has this amazing ability, unlike almost all other forms of organized crime that I know of. Essentially, there is no limit to the amount of money that a criminal gang can make out of this. So there is no reason for criminal gangs to compete. The more they collaborate with each other, the more elaborate the schemes can get and the more money they can claim. So you ended up with this essentially, it seems to have grown to been discovered by accident by mobile phone vendors in the 1990s, who then realized that there was this unbelievable golden goose that they could just keep milking, if that's what you do with geese, keep egging for golden eggs consistently. And they kept going for absolutely ages. I mean, you know, some of them carousel fraudsters became on the British rich list of the richest people in the country because they made so much money out of it. But essentially that the flaw in it is that the fact that you can import something without paying VAT and then you can claim the VAT back when you export it. And provided that there is an extra stage in that transaction, the missing trader, the person who is supposed to pay the VAT never pays it to the treasury. The person who claims it back, claims it back. And therefore you've essentially conjured up 20% of the value of a shipment from thin air. And this is why it became so expensive to the Treasury. It is an incredibly elegant form of fraud. And talking to some of the insurance adjusters who were involved in trying to work out what on earth was going on, they described this with the sort of wonder that a physicist might talk about what's happening in CERN. Because I'm talking about only two shell companies, one selling it to another that exports it. In reality, you're talking about thousands of shell companies moving that moving goods backwards and forwards, up and down. And then when it all nets out, mysteriously 20% of nothing has been created and the rest of us are on the hook for it. It is a gorgeous crime if you like crime, but it was incredibly troubling and very, very expensive and really made some bad people very wealthy.
turns.zh: 要真正解释清楚，这可能连 Odd Lots 听众的忍耐力都要撑破了。所以它叫轮播欺诈，或者叫缺失贸易商共同体内欺诈（missing trader intra-community fraud，MTIC）——一个四字母缩写，所以你能看出它是件大事。但基本上是这样的：如果你进口一件产品，比方说从 Ireland，而你在 UK，那么因为你进口了它，你不用为这笔交易缴增值税，对吧？所以没缴任何税。然后你把它卖给另一家空壳公司，这家公司由你控制，但看起来是 UK 的另一家公司。你在这笔交易上收增值税。所以你在这笔交易上加收 20%、或者不管是多少百分比的增值税。然后你把货物再出口回 Ireland。现在，如果第二家公司把货物出口出去，因为出口了，它们可以向国库（treasury）申领，可以把那 20% 再申领回来。它们能申领那 20%，是因为出口了货物就能拿到这笔钱。所以本质上你出口了它，却从没在一开始缴过它，你实际上是在申领一笔你从未缴过的增值税。所以它叫缺失贸易商共同体内欺诈，因为那个本应向国库缴增值税的贸易商就这么消失了。他们失踪了，永远不缴。所以你在申领一笔从未被缴过的税，而这有一种惊人的能力——不同于我所知道的几乎所有其他形式的有组织犯罪：本质上，一个犯罪团伙能从中赚到的钱没有上限。所以犯罪团伙之间没有理由竞争。他们彼此协作得越多，骗局就能越精密，能申领的钱就越多。于是你最终得到这个东西——它似乎是在 1990 年代被手机经销商偶然发现的，他们随后意识到有这么一只难以置信的下金蛋的鹅，可以不停地挤——如果鹅是这么用的话——不停地催它下金蛋。而且他们这么干了老长老长一段时间。我是说，你知道，一些轮播欺诈者因为从中赚了太多钱，上了 British 富人榜、成了全国最有钱的人之一。但本质上，其中的漏洞在于：你可以进口东西而不缴增值税，然后在出口时又把增值税申领回来。只要交易中有额外的一个环节——那个缺失的贸易商——本应缴增值税的人从不向国库缴，而申领回来的人则照样申领回来。因此你基本上就凭空变出了一批货物价值的 20%。这就是为什么它对国库来说代价如此高昂。它是一种极其精巧的欺诈形式。我跟一些参与查明到底发生了什么的保险理赔员（insurance adjusters）聊过，他们描述这件事时带着一种物理学家谈论 CERN 里发生什么时可能有的那种惊叹。因为我讲的只是两家空壳公司，一家卖给另一家、后者出口。而在现实中，你说的是成千上万家空壳公司，把货物来回、上下地倒腾。然后当这一切净额结算时，神秘地，凭空创造出了'无中生有'的 20%，而我们其余的人得为此买单。如果你喜欢犯罪的话，它是一桩华丽的罪行，但它极其令人不安、非常非常昂贵，而且真的让一些坏人变得非常富有。

turns.en: So obviously we've touched on a number of different, I guess, vehicles for how money gets laundered. What is the official reason for why, given everything that we know, governments... continue to produce lots of cash and particularly high denomination units of currency.
turns.zh: 所以显然我们已经谈到了若干种不同的、我想是资金被洗白的载体。那么，鉴于我们所知道的这一切，政府……继续大量生产现金、尤其是大面额货币单位的官方理由是什么？

turns.en: Yeah, I am fascinated by it. This is called the paradox of banknotes, what you described at the beginning. It was first identified formally by Andrew Bailey, now the governor of the Bank of England, back then the chief cashier, so in charge of physical coins and notes back in 2009. And it is this very strange phenomenon whereby cash is an analog technology like videotapes or films and cameras that is being out-competed by digital means of payment. Really a very small proportion of transactions are now used cash. I think it's something like 9% now in the UK, maybe 13% in the US. It's very few. So there is very little demand for cash from society. So you would expect, therefore, the supply of cash to be collapsing. And yet at the same time that the demand is very low, For some reason, supply is very, very high and getting higher all the time, consistently, almost everywhere. The amount of cash in circulation is hitting record highs in the US. It's almost 2.5 trillion US dollars in circulation. I was hoping it would hit. 2.5 trillion in time for the 250th anniversary, because it would have had a sort of nerdy appropriateness, but it didn't quite get there. But still, it's not far off in the Eurozone. It's something like 1.6 trillion euros. In the UK, it's about 100 billion pounds. So, you know, huge quantities of banknotes are being printed, and yet very few are being used. And there have been a number of proposals of suggested explanations for why this is happening. Andrew Bailey back in 2009 suggested it could be because of low inflation, that there was no real opportunity cost of holding banknotes, because why bother putting them in the bank when interest rates are so low? Another explanation was there were just lots of ATMs. So maybe the banknotes were just as it were piling up in the ATMs, and that's where they were. Another explanation was trust in financial institutions was very low, because it was immediately after the great financial crisis. Yeah, I think we can say certainly, certainly the number of ATMs is lower now than it was back then. And inflation has obviously gone up again. And you hope that the trust in financial institutions has at least partly returned in the last couple of decades. And yet the phenomenon has continued. In fact, it's accelerated, if anything, since then. The value of pounds in circulation, for example, has doubled since he made that speech. So, you know, there is clearly another reason for it. And central bankers tend to now just fall back on saying that it's a store of value.
turns.zh: 是啊，我对此非常着迷。这就叫钞票悖论（paradox of banknotes），也就是你在开头描述的那个现象。它最早是由 Andrew Bailey 正式提出的——他现在是 Bank of England 的行长，当时是首席出纳（chief cashier），也就是负责实物硬币和钞票的人——那是在 2009 年。这是一种非常奇怪的现象：现金是一种模拟（analog）技术，就像录像带、胶卷和相机一样，正在被数字支付方式击败。现在真正用现金进行的交易只占很小一部分。我想在 UK 现在大概是 9% 左右，在 US 也许 13%。非常少。所以社会对现金的需求很小。因此你会预期现金的供给在崩塌。然而就在需求很低的同时，不知为何，供给却非常非常高，而且几乎在所有地方都在持续、不断走高。在美国，流通中的现金量正创下历史新高。流通中差不多有 2.5 万亿美元。我曾希望它能赶在 250 周年国庆前达到 2.5 万亿，因为那会有种书呆子式的恰当感，但它没完全到。不过也差不远了。在 Eurozone，大约是 1.6 万亿欧元。在 UK，大约 1000 亿英镑。所以你知道，海量的钞票被印出来，却很少被使用。针对为什么会这样，已经有人提出了若干解释。Andrew Bailey 在 2009 年提出，可能是因为低通胀，持有钞票没有真正的机会成本（opportunity cost），因为利率这么低，何必把钱存进银行？另一种解释是 ATM 就是很多。所以也许钞票只是仿佛堆积在 ATM 里，就待在那儿。还有一种解释是对金融机构的信任非常低，因为那正好是 great financial crisis（大金融危机）之后。是啊，我想我们可以肯定地说，ATM 的数量现在肯定比那时候少了。通胀显然又上去了。你也希望过去几十年里对金融机构的信任至少部分回归了。然而这个现象仍在持续。事实上，如果有什么变化的话，它从那以后还加速了。比如说，流通中英镑的价值自他发表那次演讲以来已经翻了一倍。所以你知道，显然还有另一个原因。而央行官员们现在往往只能退回到说它是一种价值储藏（store of value）。

turns.en: That.
turns.zh: 那个。

turns.en: There are two basic uses for money, really. It's either a medium of exchange or it's a store of value. Those are the two options. And since it's not being used as a medium of exchange, then they said, well, it's presumably being used as a store of value. And that's what they tend to come up with. And that's really frustrating because you can see from the surveys that central banks do that it isn't being used as a store of value. The average American adult has, I think, something like $ 430 odd either on their person or at home at any one time. And yet there's more than $ 7, 000 out there for every man, woman, and child in the United States. It's an order of magnitude higher than the amount that's being used as a store of value. And yet there is no attempt really by central bankers to explain why that's happening. You know, what's going on? Where are all the banknotes? I mean, they do efforts to try and work out how many of them are outside the country. There's an economist at the Fed called Ruth Judson, who's done some really interesting work on this, and then another colleague at the European Central Bank. And the European Central Bank reckons about half of Euro banknotes are outside the Eurozone. The Fed reckons sort of something like 65%, maybe, of dollar banknotes are outside the United States. But that's just a kind of a way of kicking the problem one step further. If it's a store of value outside the United States, it's still must be being used for something and yet what is it well essentially we don't know they never really the central bank has certainly never really answered that question of where are all this astonishing quantity of banknotes that they're printing and it is a really interesting puzzle i mean if you imagine that this was not banknotes that we're talking about but was vhs cassettes um that Netflix has boomed, everyone's watching Disney +, and yet somehow VHS cassette production is hitting record highs year after year after year. I think we'd be really interested in where they were going. Who's watching all these things? And yet just because it's banknotes, everyone's like, oh, well, it's a store of value. Forget about it.
turns.zh: 钱其实有两种基本用途。要么是交易媒介（medium of exchange），要么是价值储藏。就这两个选项。既然它没有被当作交易媒介使用，那他们说，嗯，它大概是被当作价值储藏在用了。这就是他们往往给出的说法。而这真的很令人沮丧，因为从央行做的那些调查中你能看出，它并没有被当作价值储藏使用。美国成年人在任一时点，随身或放在家里的现金，我想大概是 430 美元出头。然而在外面，United States 每个男人、女人和孩子对应超过 7000 美元。这比被用作价值储藏的金额高出一个数量级。然而央行官员们根本没有试图解释为什么会这样。你知道，到底怎么回事？所有这些钞票都在哪儿？我是说，他们确实有努力去弄清楚其中有多少在国外。Fed 有一位经济学家叫 Ruth Judson，她在这方面做了一些非常有意思的研究，然后 European Central Bank 还有另一位同事。European Central Bank 估计大约一半的欧元钞票在 Eurozone 之外。Fed 估计大概有 65% 左右的美元钞票在 United States 之外。但那只是把问题往后踢了一步。如果它是 United States 之外的价值储藏，它仍然一定是被用来做了某种用途，可那用途是什么？嗯，本质上我们不知道。他们从来没有——央行当然从来没有真正回答过那个问题：他们印出来的这惊人数量钞票到底都在哪儿？这真是个非常有意思的谜题。我是说，如果你想象我们谈论的不是钞票，而是 VHS 录像带——Netflix 已经火爆起来，人人都在看 Disney+，然而不知为何 VHS 录像带的产量却年复一年创下历史新高。我想我们会非常想知道它们都去了哪儿。谁在看这些东西？然而就因为它是钞票，人人都说，哦，好吧，那是价值储藏。别管它了。

turns.en: Can you talk to us about seniorage? So this is one of these concepts where it comes up occasionally and I sort of nod my head and I go, yes, of course central banks make money by distributing dollars, but I don't actually know how it works.
turns.zh: 你能跟我们讲讲铸币税（seigneurage）吗？这是那种偶尔会冒出来的概念，我会点点头说，是的，当然央行通过发行美元赚钱，但我其实并不知道它是怎么运作的。

turns.en: Well, so seigneurage is one of these really ancient, wonderful concepts that, I mean, so you can tell it's old because we use an actually Norman French word for it. Seigneurage means that which pertains to the seigneur or the lord, which essentially is that making money, having a monopoly on the production of money is a very profitable thing to have, which is why almost as soon as any warlord kind of took over a patch of territory and declared himself to be king, one of the first things they did was have a monopoly on issuing money. And so there's quite a lot of warlords in Anglo-Saxon England that we only know the name of because we found a few coins with their names on. Essentially, in those days, it was that if you wanted to have your money coined, you had to bring it to the mint, where the king would put his face on it and take a little bit for his trouble. That's the origin of the term seigneurage. But in the modern sense, obviously, we don't use gold so much anymore. It's just paper. In the modern term, it's the profit that is made from issuing paper money. And there are two ways of looking at this. There's a sort of simple but wrong way and a right but complicated way so the simple but wrong way of looking at this is that it's very cheap to print money it costs about nine cents to print a hundred dollar bill you know the there's whatever 20 20 billion us dollar bills out there somewhere so you know if you think about that each one costs nine cents to print you can see that there's a 99.9 99.91 margin on producing them that's a very profitable thing that's your seniorage right there the fact that you're making $ 99. 91 every time you print a $ 100 bill. So that's the simple but wrong way of looking at it. And central bankers will tell you this is wrong. Because actually, a $ 100 bill, if you take a $ 100 bill out the bank, you're not actually buying that $ 100 bill because you can sell it back at any time for the same amount that you bought it for. So actually, it's an interest-free loan to the government is what it really is. And this is where we start getting towards very much the end of my maths. And I'm hoping that you guys will correct me at this point. So there's $ 2. 5 trillion US dollars out there somewhere. That's an interest-free loan to the US government, broadly understood, of $ 2. 5 trillion. Now, I think the US government debt, outstanding government debt, is something like $ 40, almost $ 40 trillion now. So $ 2. 5 trillion on top of that is like an additional, what is that, sort of 6% or something of US government debt, which the US government isn't having to pay any interest on. That's quite a significant saving for the US government not to have to pay that money. I think that as I remember rightly from the last thing I saw, I think that debt servicing now is something about 19% of the federal budget. If you had to pay interest on that extra two and a half trillion, then that's probably another percentage point on top of that. So yeah, that's quite a decent amount of money which the US government saves, essentially by having a chunk of its debt in the form of bearer instruments that don't pay interest. So that's, as it were, the right but complicated way of looking at Saini Ridge. But either way that you look at it, Saini Ridge is a very profitable thing to have, which is why governments tend to like having a monopoly on the issuing of money, because it's essentially either it's just straightforwardly profitable selling bits of paper, or it's a very cheap way of raising a loan.
turns.zh: 嗯，铸币税是那种非常古老、非常美妙的概念之一，我是说，你能看出它很古老，因为我们其实用了一个 Norman French（诺曼法语）词来称呼它。Seigneurage 的意思是'属于 seigneur 或领主的东西'，本质上就是说，制造货币、拥有货币生产的垄断权，是一件非常有利可图的事，这就是为什么几乎任何一个军阀一占领一片领土、自封为王，他们最早做的事情之一就是垄断货币发行。所以在 Anglo-Saxon England 有相当多的军阀，我们之所以知道他们的名字，仅仅是因为我们发现了几枚刻有他们名字的硬币。基本上，在那个年代，如果你想把你的钱铸成硬币，你得把它带到铸币厂（mint），国王会在上面印上他的脸，并从中抽取一小部分作为他的辛劳报酬。这就是 seigneurage 这个术语的起源。但在现代意义上，显然，我们不再那么多地使用黄金了。它只是纸。在现代术语里，它指的是发行纸币所赚取的利润。而看待这件事有两种方式。一种是简单但错误的方式，一种是正确但复杂的方式。简单但错误的方式是这样看：印钱非常便宜，印一张一百美元钞票的成本大约 9 美分，你知道，外面某处大约有 200 亿张美元钞票，所以如果你想，每一张印出来要花 9 美分，你能看出生产它们有 99.91 的利润率——那可是非常赚钱的买卖，那就是你的铸币税：你每印一张 100 美元钞票就赚 99.91 美元。所以那是简单但错误的看法。而央行官员会告诉你这是错的。因为实际上，一张 100 美元钞票——如果你从银行取出一张 100 美元钞票，你其实并没有'买'下那张 100 美元钞票，因为你随时可以用你买入时的同样金额把它卖回去。所以实际上，它真正是对政府的一笔无息贷款（interest-free loan）。而这就开始逼近我数学能力的极限了。我希望你们两位在这点上纠正我。所以外面某处有 2.5 万亿美元。宽泛地理解，那就是对 US 政府的一笔 2.5 万亿美元的无息贷款。现在，我想 US 政府债务、未偿政府债务大约是 40 万亿、将近 40 万亿美元了。所以在此之上的 2.5 万亿美元，就相当于额外的——那是多少来着——大约 US 政府债务的 6% 左右，而 US 政府无需为此支付任何利息。对 US 政府来说，不用付这笔钱是相当可观的一笔节省。我记得没错的话，从我上次看到的，我想现在偿债（debt servicing）大约占联邦预算的 19%。如果你不得不对那额外的 2.5 万亿付利息，那大概会在其上再加一个百分点。所以是的，那是相当可观的一笔钱，US 政府基本上是通过让自己的一部分债务以不付利息的无记名票据形式存在而省下来的。所以这，可以说是看待铸币税的正确但复杂的方式。但无论你以哪种方式看，铸币税都是一件非常有利可图的事，这就是为什么政府往往喜欢拥有货币发行的垄断权，因为它本质上要么是卖纸片直截了当地赚钱，要么是一种极其廉价的举债方式。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So just to repeat Joe's question then, politically, who is actually blocking getting rid of, for instance, $ 100 bills? Would it be central banks and the Treasury protecting seniorage, or is it simple inertia or is it maybe tax avoidant industries, the powerful nail salon and, I don't know, psychic reader in New York lobby or something like that?
turns.zh: 那就重复一下 Joe 的问题：在政治层面，究竟是谁在阻挠废除、比如说 100 美元钞票？是央行和财政部（Treasury）在保护铸币税，还是单纯的惯性，又或者也许是那些避税的行业——New York 那些强大的美甲沙龙，还有，我不知道，通灵占卜师之类的游说团体？

turns.en: I think broadly speaking, this doesn't come up. The system from the perspective of the European Central Bank or the Fed or the Bank of England or the Bank of Canada, the system is working fine. There's lots and lots of demand for their products. Why would you want to get rid of them? If you look at it more broadly and you work out that essentially the products are enabling crime on a geopolitical scale, then you would say, well, actually, the harm that's being caused far outweighs the profits that's coming from the Seigneur, which we should do something about this. But essentially, these are different bits of government, and they don't necessarily talk to each other. There have been occasions in the past when governments have got rid of big bills to try and reduce criminality or terrorism. After the attacks on Paris in 2016, the Europeans announced that they weren't going to produce, they used to have a 500 euro bill which was referred to colloquially as the Bin Laden, because everyone had heard of it, but no one had seen it. And by the time one of your banknotes has been called the Bin Laden, you know that you're in a degree of trouble. That's not a good nickname to have.
turns.zh: 我认为大体来说，这个问题根本不会被提上议程。从 European Central Bank、Fed、Bank of England 或 Bank of Canada 的角度看，这个系统运转得很好。它们的产品有大量的需求。你为什么要废掉它们？如果你更宽泛地看，并弄明白这些产品本质上是在助长地缘政治规模的犯罪，那你就会说，嗯，实际上，造成的危害远远超过从铸币税中来的利润，我们应该为此做点什么。但本质上，这些是政府里不同的部门，它们未必会互相沟通。过去也曾有过政府为减少犯罪或恐怖主义而废除大面额钞票的时候。在 2016 年 Paris 遇袭之后，Europeans 宣布他们将不再生产——他们过去有一种 500 欧元钞票，俗称'Bin Laden'，因为人人都听说过它，却没人见过它。而当你的一张钞票被叫做 Bin Laden 时，你就知道你多少有点麻烦了。那可不是个好绰号。

turns.en: That's the first hint.
turns.zh: 那是第一个征兆。

turns.en: Singapore used to have a big bill as well, I think a $ 10, 000 bill, which they got rid of. But broadly speaking, you've got a kind of collective action problem, which is that if the US stops producing its $ 100 bill, and I wish it would, I don't think that there is anyone really, who would be inconvenienced by the lack of $ 100 bills except the bad guys.
turns.zh: Singapore 过去也有一种大面额钞票，我想是 1 万美元（新元）的钞票，他们把它废除了。但大体来说，你面对的是一种集体行动难题（collective action problem）：如果 US 停止生产它的 100 美元钞票——我倒希望它这么做——我不认为除了坏人之外，真的会有谁因为没有 100 美元钞票而感到不便。

turns.en: Music video producers.
turns.zh: 音乐录影带制作人。

turns.en: Well, yeah, music video producers. I mean, I suppose what would hip hop artists wave around in their music videos? But leaving that aside, the Europeans would still be producing 100 euro and 200 euro banknotes. And then the Americans would then essentially lose out on the seniorage to the Europeans. And the criminal economy would get no smaller because they would just switch to using euros instead and vice versa. There are enough central banks producing big bills, whether that's a 50 pound note or a thousand franc note or 200 euros, a hundred dollar bill, that if one of them went out the game, it essentially wouldn't make that much difference to the criminals, but would make a substantial difference to their own income from this. So what you need is an international agreement that everyone could get together and say, we're not going to do this. And that's what has been eluding humanity. Well, in this, as in so many other ways, when it comes to to try to tackle financial crime. Because if you are the person, jurisdiction that is enabling financial crime is actually quite profitable for you personally. The city of London has been doing quite well out of this for decades. And most of the harm is then spread elsewhere in the world. So you get the profit and other people get the harm. And the fact that the hundred dollar bills are the favorite tool of the cartels in Colombia and Mexico is very bad for Colombia and Mexico, but it's also quite profitable for the United States. So that's the The essential challenge is trying to persuade people that they all need to act together. And that's something that, well, no one's really tried it, but even the vague suggestions. And some economists have talked about this in the past. Kenneth Rogoff has talked about this at length and tried to get interest for this idea. He's really come up against the challenge of trying to get everyone in a room together to agree.
turns.zh: 嗯，是啊，音乐录影带制作人。我是说，我想 hip hop 艺人在他们的音乐录影带里还能挥什么呢？但撇开这个不谈，Europeans 仍然会生产 100 欧元和 200 欧元钞票。那样的话，Americans 本质上就会把铸币税输给 Europeans。而犯罪经济一点都不会缩小，因为他们只会转而用欧元，反之亦然。生产大面额钞票的央行足够多——不管是 50 英镑钞票、1000 法郎钞票、200 欧元，还是 100 美元钞票——以至于如果其中一家退出这场游戏，本质上对罪犯没多大影响，却会对它自己从中获得的收入产生重大影响。所以你所需要的，是一份国际协议，让大家聚在一起说，我们不干这个了。而这正是人类一直没能做到的——在打击金融犯罪这件事上，就像在很多其他方面一样。因为如果你就是那个助长金融犯罪的人、司法辖区，这对你个人其实相当有利可图。City of London（伦敦金融城）几十年来一直从中获益颇丰。而大部分危害则被扩散到世界其他地方。所以你得到利润，别人承受危害。而 100 美元钞票是 Colombia 和 Mexico 贩毒集团最青睐的工具这一事实，对 Colombia 和 Mexico 非常糟糕，但对 United States 也相当有利可图。所以这就是那个根本的挑战：试图说服所有人他们需要一起行动。而这，嗯，其实没人真正尝试过，但即便是那些含糊的提议——一些经济学家过去谈论过这个。Kenneth Rogoff 曾长篇大论地谈过，并试图为这个想法争取支持。他真的碰上了一个难题：试图把所有人聚到一个房间里达成一致。

turns.en: To do it.
turns.zh: 去做这件事。

turns.en: You know, something I realized, the Chinese currency, the highest denomination note there is 100 RMB, so only about $ 15. Also, every one of their bills has the exact same design, basically. It's the Mao photo, which I think is kind of interesting. You look around, it seems like they usually switch it up, etc., One thing I'm curious about, was crypto ever an important part of this story? I remember back then, people were like, oh, it's going to be used for money laundering and stuff. And I thought that the crypto people made a good point. It's like, look at the banks and the cash you're producing. That's where most of the action is happening. Obviously, crypto isn't really like what it was, at least a few years ago, et cetera. But during that period, did it ever really move the dial as a vehicle?
turns.zh: 你知道，我意识到一件事，Chinese 货币里，最高面额的钞票是 100 RMB，也就是只有大约 15 美元。而且，他们每一张钞票基本上都完全是同样的设计。就是 Mao 的照片，我觉得这挺有意思。你环顾四周，似乎各国通常会换着花样设计之类的。我好奇的一件事是，加密货币（crypto）曾经是这个故事里重要的一部分吗？我记得那时候，人们说，哦，它会被用来洗钱之类的。而我觉得 crypto 那帮人提出了一个很好的观点。就像，看看银行和你们生产的那些现金吧。大部分的动作都发生在那里。显然，crypto 现在已经不是它几年前的样子了，等等。但在那段时期，作为一种载体，它有没有真正改变过局面？

turns.en: I mean, crypto is huge for money laundering. Specifically, there are many cryptos. You know, it's not just one thing. Specifically, we're really talking about stable coins when we talk about crypto being big in money laundering. I was talking earlier about trade-based money laundering and how essentially you can move value via moving stuff, whether that's Caterpillar, earth-moving equipment or handbags or drugs or whatever around the world. And you move value in that shape like the Medici's used to. Crypto allows you to do that instantaneously. So the really entrepreneurial money laundering gangs now tend to, and this is the Russians, the Chinese, the Iranians do this too. They combine cash and crypto. So cash works at a street level and then you collect the cash and you exchange it for crypto. And then the crypto is useful. for moving your wealth around the world, for buying product from Colombia or elsewhere. So the two are not exclusive. In fact, they supercharge each other. Criminals have always liked to stack different techniques on top of each other. And so, yeah, cash remains the most useful criminal tool at a street level. But it's bulky, it's not secure. It's kind of annoying and smelly. It's annoying to count and so on. So if you can get away from using that as quickly as possible in order to move it around the world, that's where crypto comes in and is super useful. The Russians have created their own cryptocurrency, A7A5, although it's in a little bit of trouble at the moment, essentially as a way of allowing themselves to do this outside of the Western controlled stablecoins. But there are other Western controlled stablecoins that are available, which I'm sure you have spoken about on the podcast. In fact, I know you.
turns.zh: 我是说，加密货币在洗钱方面是巨大的。具体来说，有很多种 crypto。你知道，它不只是单一的东西。具体来说，当我们谈论 crypto 在洗钱里分量很重时，我们真正说的是稳定币（stablecoins）。我前面谈到基于贸易的洗钱，以及本质上你如何通过转移货物——不管是 Caterpillar 土方设备、手袋、毒品还是别的什么——来在全球转移价值。你以那种方式转移价值，就像 Medici 家族过去做的一样。而 crypto 让你能瞬间做到这一点。所以现在真正有创业精神的洗钱团伙往往会——Russians、Chinese、Iranians 也这么干——他们把现金和 crypto 结合起来。所以现金在街头层面管用，然后你把现金收上来，换成 crypto。接着 crypto 就有用了，用于把你的财富转移到世界各地，用于从 Colombia 或其他地方买货。所以这两者并不互斥。事实上，它们相互增强。罪犯一直喜欢把不同的技术层层叠加在一起。所以，是啊，现金在街头层面仍然是最有用的犯罪工具。但它笨重、不安全。它有点烦人、还有味道。数起来很烦人，等等。所以如果你能尽快摆脱使用它、以便把它转移到世界各地，那就是 crypto 派上用场、而且超级有用的地方。Russians 创造了他们自己的加密货币 A7A5，尽管它眼下有点麻烦，本质上作为一种让他们自己能在西方控制的稳定币之外做这件事的方式。但也有其他可用的、西方控制的稳定币，我相信你们在播客里谈到过。事实上，我知道你们谈过。

turns.en: You know, you mentioned earlier this idea that if the US got rid of $ 100 bills, then maybe everyone would just start using 200 euro bills or something like that. I'm curious in your discussions, you must have had some with money launderers or people who investigate money laundering. Do you hear a lot about, I'm trying to think what to say, fraudsters thinking about the actual like value of the currency or making currency hedging decisions? So like, I don't want dollars because I think the dollar is going to go down. I'm going to move into euros instead. Or is it just purely about the use case and some broader utilitarian diversification kind of thing?
turns.zh: 你知道，你前面提到了这个想法：如果 US 废除了 100 美元钞票，那也许大家就会开始用 200 欧元钞票之类的。我很好奇，在你的讨论中——你一定跟洗钱者或调查洗钱的人有过一些交流——你经常听到，我在想该怎么说，骗子们考虑货币的实际价值、或者做货币对冲（currency hedging）决策吗？比如说，'我不想要美元，因为我觉得美元要跌，我要转而持有欧元。'还是说这纯粹是关于使用场景、以及某种更宽泛的、功利性的分散化（diversification）之类的事情？

turns.en: I would love that if there was... I mean, I used to live in Russia and it's how I got into writing about financial crime was living in Russia. I mean, the good thing about working in Russia as a journalist is you don't really need to look out for financial crime. It tends to come and find you. And it was that there was a really... deep awareness of the relative strengths of the euro and the dollar. And this was a time when the euro was looking very strong. And so there was a movement towards euros by ordinary Russians. But you can't get away from the fact that the dollar is just much more liquid a market. It's much more widely accepted. And it was interesting. It actually used to get different exchange rates for different kinds of dollars. When I first lived in Russia, I was paid in cash dollars. And I would always try and be paid in $ 100 bills because I knew I could get more rubles. for a $ 100 bill than I could for a 20, because there's that demand for hundreds. So no, I mean, dollars were that the utility of dollars was more about the universal application of them, the fact they're accepted everywhere. And because as you say, there is a 200 euro banknote, you can move twice the value in the same space with euros as you can with dollars. But because the dollar has got this kind of first mover advantage, and it's globally accepted, the dollar remains the lingua franca of global criminality, the $ 100 bill, just because it is a much deeper, more liquid market, which has an interesting, obviously an interesting parallel to the role of the dollar as a global currency in the licit economy, which is that it has all of the instruments built up around it. Everyone trusts it. Everyone knows it. And it is very difficult to dislodge that once it's been established.
turns.zh: 如果真有那种情况我倒是很乐意……我是说，我过去住在 Russia，而我之所以开始写金融犯罪，正是因为住在 Russia。我是说，作为一名记者在 Russia 工作的好处是，你其实不需要去留意金融犯罪。它往往会主动找上门来。而且当时人们对欧元和美元的相对强弱有一种非常……深刻的认识。那是欧元看起来非常强势的时候。所以普通 Russians 有一股转向欧元的潮流。但你没法回避这样一个事实：美元的市场流动性要大得多，被接受得广泛得多。而且很有意思的是，不同种类的美元其实能换到不同的汇率。我刚住在 Russia 时，是拿现金美元发工资的。我总是设法拿 100 美元钞票，因为我知道一张 100 美元钞票能换到的卢布比一张 20 美元的多，因为对百元钞有那么大的需求。所以，不，我是说，美元的用处更多在于它们的普适性、在于它们到处都被接受这个事实。而且正如你所说，因为有一种 200 欧元钞票，你用欧元在同样空间里能转移的价值是用美元的两倍。但因为美元有这种先发优势（first mover advantage），而且全球通用，美元——那张 100 美元钞票——仍然是全球犯罪界的通用语（lingua franca），就因为它是一个深得多、流动性大得多的市场，这显然跟美元作为合法经济（licit economy）中全球货币的角色有一个有意思的相似之处：它周围建立了所有的金融工具。人人都信任它。人人都认识它。而一旦确立，就很难把它撼动。

turns.en: Yeah, just a last question for me. You mentioned the rise of some of these acts in the 70s and 80s to clamp down on money laundering, etc., Has the political climate changed? What was the political climate then such that there was an inspiration to really try to move on this? And would you just say we're in an environment today where there is just, it's just not, most people, most countries don't care very much and they have other things to worry about. And there isn't really the appetite to do another push, even if the reporting says there's quite a bit of it out there.
turns.zh: 是啊，就我最后一个问题。你提到 70、80 年代出台了一些法案来打击洗钱等等。政治气候变了吗？当时的政治气候是怎样的，以至于有一种动力去真正推动这件事？你会不会说，我们今天所处的环境就是——它就是不……大多数人、大多数国家不太在意，他们有别的更要紧的事要操心。而且即便报道说外面还有相当多的洗钱活动，也没有真正再推一把的意愿了。

turns.en: I'm really glad you asked that because it gives me the opportunity to bring up my personal anti-money laundering hero, who's a guy called Wright Patman, who was a congressman from Northeastern Texas, who represented Texarkana in the area around there. From the 1928 up to 1974, he was one of those imperfect but amazing Southern Democrats. He was, by Southern Democrat standards, a really good guy, but not necessarily a really good guy by everyone's standards today. But he did have a very healthy distrust of monopoly power, financial institutions, which grew out of this sort of what was called the populist movement in Texas and the South and the Midwest in the late 19th century. And he really, as chair of the House Banking Committee in the 1960s, he pushed through some really interesting committee hearings and innovations. And so the anti-money laundering legislation was called the Bank Secrecy Act, even though that's not its proper name, grew out of his personal kind of obsession with the wrongdoing of the financial institutions. And because of the kind of the way that Congress was very hierarchical back then, what the Banking Committee did, then Congress tended to go along with. He had a huge amount of personal power and prestige that allowed him to do that. And I'm not sure that that would be replicatable today. The role that he played, though, I think in a way is sort of, in some ways, you could see similarities with, say, the role that Elizabeth Warren played with consumer finance after the great financial crisis. He managed to push through some changes and spearhead that. So There was an opportunity back then with the growth of offshore finance in the 1960s, and he took that opportunity to bring the Bank Secrecy Act onto the books. So it is difficult to see who would fill the position that he filled now. I mean, that kind of politician isn't really present, but who knows? Things move fast. And I personally would like to see politicians engaging with the minutiae of money laundering in the same way that he did, and trying not to just, as it were, punt responsibility onto the banks and say... that they just need to produce another 100,000 suspicious transaction reports and instead say, well, actually, what does money laundering really look like? How do we tackle money laundering using crypto? How do we tackle money laundering using handbags or earth moving equipment? What is actually going on? What's really driving this? Because we have a status quo that is incredibly expensive, very intrusive. We haven't talked about debanking, but that is a serious issue, both in politics, but I think more broadly, globally. that affects hundreds of thousands of people, mostly Muslims, but others too, as a really grotesque side effect of anti-money laundering and anti-terrorist financing restrictions. It's very expensive, and it really doesn't work. So we're putting a lot of expense on financial institutions, and therefore on ourselves, and not really inconveniencing criminals to any meaningful extent. And one of the reasons why we're not inconveniencing them is because while governments are putting these very expensive regulations onto financial institutions, they are simultaneously printing essentially limitless quantities of banknotes that are allowing criminals to evade those same restrictions by just using cash. So it is an incredibly frustrating situation to look at. And to be honest, it just makes me furious most of the time.
turns.zh: 我真的很高兴你问这个，因为它给了我一个机会，来提一提我个人的反洗钱英雄，一个名叫 Wright Patman 的人，他是来自 Northeastern Texas 的一位国会议员，代表 Texarkana 及其周边地区。从 1928 年一直到 1974 年。他是那种不完美但了不起的 Southern Democrats（南方民主党人）之一。以南方民主党人的标准看，他是个非常好的人，但以今天所有人的标准看，未必算个非常好的人。但他确实对垄断权力、对金融机构有一种非常健康的怀疑，这源自 19 世纪末在 Texas、南方和中西部所谓的民粹主义运动（populist movement）。而作为 1960 年代众议院银行委员会（House Banking Committee）的主席，他真的推动通过了一些非常有意思的委员会听证和创新。所以那部反洗钱立法——被称为 Bank Secrecy Act，尽管那不是它的正式名称——正是源于他个人对金融机构不当行为的一种执念。而且由于当时国会非常等级化的运作方式，银行委员会做的事，国会往往就会跟着走。他拥有巨大的个人权力和威望，让他能做到这一点。我不确定这在今天是否还能复制。不过，他所扮演的角色，我觉得在某种意义上，你可以看到它与——比如说——Elizabeth Warren 在 great financial crisis 之后在消费金融领域所扮演角色的相似之处。他设法推动通过了一些变革并牵头去做。所以在 1960 年代，随着离岸金融（offshore finance）的增长，当时有一个机会，他抓住了这个机会，把 Bank Secrecy Act 写进了法典。所以现在很难看出谁能填补他所填补的那个位置。我是说，那种政客其实已经不太存在了，但谁知道呢？世事变化很快。而我个人希望看到政客们像他那样去钻研洗钱的细枝末节，不要只是、可以说是把责任甩给银行，说……他们只需要再多产出 10 万份可疑交易报告，而是应该说，嗯，实际上，洗钱到底长什么样？我们如何打击利用 crypto 的洗钱？我们如何打击利用手袋或土方设备的洗钱？到底在发生什么？真正在驱动这一切的是什么？因为我们有一个极其昂贵、非常侵扰性的现状。我们还没谈到去银行化（debanking），但那是个严重的问题，无论是在政治层面，我想更广泛地说，在全球层面。它影响到成千上万的人，主要是 Muslims，但也有其他人，作为反洗钱和反恐融资限制的一个极其怪诞的副作用。它非常昂贵，而且真的不起作用。所以我们把大量成本压在金融机构身上、因而也压在我们自己身上，却没有在任何有意义的程度上真正给罪犯造成不便。而我们之所以没能给他们造成不便，原因之一是：各国政府在把这些极其昂贵的监管压到金融机构身上的同时，又在印制本质上无限量、让罪犯能够仅仅通过使用现金就绕开那些同样限制的钞票。所以这是一种极其令人沮丧的局面。老实说，大多数时候它只会让我愤怒。

turns.en: How would you actually change the incentive structure for banks? I'm thinking of like Some poor compliance officer sitting in a basement somewhere, and he's filing thousands of suspicious activity reports, knowing that they're probably going to go into some black hole that no one is ever going to read. And at the same time, it's not like the bank is getting rewarded for filing all of those. It's all downside, right? If you miss something and you get caught, then you're in trouble. So it feels like something could be improved on that side of things.
turns.zh: 你实际上会怎么改变银行的激励结构？我想的是，某个可怜的合规官（compliance officer）坐在某处的地下室里，提交着成千上万份可疑活动报告，明知它们很可能要掉进某个没人会去读的黑洞。与此同时，银行并不会因为提交了所有这些报告而得到奖励。全是下行风险，对吧？如果你漏掉了什么又被抓到，那就有麻烦了。所以感觉在那一面上，有些东西是可以改进的。

turns.en: The original idea with Suspicious... activity reports, which grew out of the creation of the Financial Action Task Force at the Paris G7 in 1989, the original idea would they would be a source of real time intelligence for law enforcement agencies, that they would receive these reports that would allow them to essentially see money laundering as it was happening. And for that to work, you need to have enough people to read the reports, you need to have essentially effective software systems that can take in the reports and kind of triage them to the places where they need to go. And that's what we don't have, that there has been this demand on financial institutions to hire tens of thousands of compliance officers who sit there bashing out reports for false negatives endlessly or false positives. And it's just incredibly laborious, bureaucratic and tiresome work. But at the same time, most countries don't actually, no countries really resource their law enforcement agencies sufficiently to actually read the reports that are being produced. So you have, like you say, huge number of reports that are just going into essentially a black hole where they sit there and maybe they'll be looked at in the future and maybe they won't. And the downside of getting it wrong for a financial institution is a billion dollar, billion dollar plus fine. And the plus side of getting it right is kind of non-existent. So in terms of changing the incentives, it would be far better to have fewer suspicious activity reports that were actually being read. And then you could have a system where financial criminals were actually being prosecuted and you would get a sort of a kind of feedback loop that that would then restrict the ability of their financial criminals to move their money because the whole idea of an anti-money laundering system is to try and take the profit out of financial crime or any acquisitive crime that's what they're trying to do is to make it expensive to launder money that's what we're failing to do at the moment yeah so anything that can take away criminals money and essentially take away their ability to move it so easily around the world that would essentially be the purpose. And that is supposedly the purpose of the system that we have. Instead, we have a system that piles a huge amount of paperwork on financial institutions and a huge amount of expense and occasionally fines them for their trouble, but doesn't really do anything to stop financial crime. And that's kind of, as we say in Britain, ass backwards.
turns.zh: 可疑……活动报告最初的想法——它源于 1989 年 Paris G7 上 Financial Action Task Force 的创立——最初的设想是，它们会成为执法机构的实时情报来源，让他们能收到这些报告，从而基本上能看到洗钱正在发生。而要让这一点奏效，你需要有足够多的人去读这些报告，你本质上需要有有效的软件系统，能接收这些报告并把它们分诊（triage）到该去的地方。而这正是我们所缺乏的：一直以来对金融机构有这样的要求，雇用数以万计的合规官，坐在那儿不停地赶制报告，处理无穷无尽的漏报（false negatives）或误报（false positives）。而这只是极其费力、官僚化、令人厌倦的工作。但与此同时，大多数国家其实——没有哪个国家真正给自己的执法机构提供了足够的资源，去真正阅读这些被产出的报告。所以就像你说的，你有海量的报告，只是掉进一个黑洞，躺在那里，也许将来会被看一看，也许不会。而对一家金融机构来说，搞砸的下行风险是十亿美元、十亿以上的罚款。而搞对了的上行好处则几乎不存在。所以在改变激励方面，与其如此，不如少一些可疑活动报告、但真正被阅读，那要好得多。然后你就能有一套系统，金融罪犯真正被起诉，你就会得到一种反馈循环（feedback loop），进而限制金融罪犯转移资金的能力，因为整个反洗钱系统的理念，就是要试图把利润从金融犯罪、或任何牟利型犯罪中拿走——他们想做的就是让洗钱变得昂贵——而这正是我们此刻没能做到的。是啊，所以任何能拿走罪犯的钱、本质上拿走他们如此轻易地在全球转移资金的能力的东西，那基本上就是目的所在。而那本该是我们现有系统的目的。相反，我们却有一套系统，把海量文书和巨额成本堆到金融机构头上，偶尔还因为它们'辛苦'而罚款，却对阻止金融犯罪几乎毫无作为。这就有点——用我们 British 人的话说——完全搞反了（ass backwards）。

turns.en: All right. I think that's a good place to end it. Oliver Bullough, thank you so much for coming on All Thoughts.
turns.zh: 好。我觉得这是一个不错的收尾之处。Oliver Bullough，非常感谢你来上 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Thanks for having me on the show.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我上节目。

turns.en: Thank you, Oliver. That was great.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Oliver。太精彩了。

turns.en: Great. So Joe, that was a fun conversation.
turns.zh: 太好了。Joe，那真是一段有意思的对话。

turns.en: Yeah, I love reading about the intricacies of all these details and the complexity and how.
turns.zh: 是啊，我喜欢读所有这些细节的错综复杂、以及那种复杂性和如何……

turns.en: Far- There's a lot of creativity in crime.
turns.zh: 走得多远——犯罪中有很多创造力。

turns.en: Extraordinary amount of creativity. And it's like, okay, you come up with one idea where you can sort of, it's like they found a free money glitch in the tax system where you import something, have one transaction, then claim the refund, et cetera. And then it's like finding these ways to do it across thousands and thousands of companies or fake companies, whatever it is. It's always very impressive to me.
turns.zh: 非凡的创造力。而且就像，好，你想出一个点子，可以某种——就像他们在税制里发现了一个免费拿钱的漏洞（glitch），你进口某样东西，做一笔交易，然后申领退款，等等。然后又像是找到跨越成千上万家公司、或假公司之类去做这件事的方法，不管是什么。这总是让我印象深刻。

turns.en: With carousel fraud, though, I keep thinking, like, okay, sure, it makes you rich, right?
turns.zh: 不过说到轮播欺诈，我一直在想，好，当然，它让你变富，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But your job is basically filing a bunch of paperwork and incorporating a bunch of shell companies, which sounds really, really boring.
turns.zh: 但你的工作基本上就是提交一堆文书、注册一堆空壳公司，这听起来真的、真的很无聊。

turns.en: So you think the problem is, like, it makes you rich, but it provides you no meaning in life?
turns.zh: 所以你觉得问题在于，它让你变富，却不给你的人生提供任何意义？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I think, like, why not just start a business, right? Do something interesting. Don't just make money by, like, creating shell companies. I don't know.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说，我觉得，为什么不干脆去创办一家企业呢，对吧？做点有意思的事。别只是靠创建空壳公司来赚钱。我不知道。

turns.en: I think people can find ways to enjoy themselves with just lots and lots of free money. You know, it's interesting. I've thought about this before when he was talking about the way criminals, as he called it, stack cash and crypto. And something I've thought about, and I think there's a lot, there's actually sort of like common, even when he described a sort of like classically Medici style banking system or whatever, how many transactions that we think of as like being somewhat bilateral transactions are actually like very multi-step. So let's say you wanted to sell me a painting and I was like, oh, I'll pay it for you in Bitcoin. Or like, I don't really see that happening, but it's like, I would have to, like that would be three transactions because there would be, I would be purchasing Bitcoin from some entity.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们能靠大把大把的免费钱找到自得其乐的方式。你知道，这很有意思。之前他谈到罪犯——用他的话说——把现金和 crypto 层层叠加时，我就想过这件事。有一点我一直在想，我觉得其实有很多、实际上算是共通的东西：即便是在他描述那种经典的 Medici 式银行系统之类的时候，有多少我们以为是某种双边交易的交易，实际上是非常多步骤的。所以比方说你想卖给我一幅画，我说，哦，我用 Bitcoin 付给你。或者说，我不太觉得那真会发生，但就像，我将不得不——那会是三笔交易，因为会有——我会从某个实体那里购买 Bitcoin。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: The one Bitcoin exchange would then like move it to your wallet. And then presumably you don't want to hold a lot of Bitcoin. So then you sell the Bitcoin for cash. So what looks like, oh, I'm going to pay you in Bitcoin is like really three transactions. three distinct movements. And I think that a lot of these things that he describes, how can you deposit money in Rome and then withdraw it as soon as you get there in London, is this nature of the fact that a lot of times what looks like a transaction is really like this big multi-leg transaction that can sort of be decompose and rearrange like Lego blocks in multiple ways.
turns.zh: 那个 Bitcoin 交易所接着会把它转到你的钱包。然后想必你不想持有大量 Bitcoin。所以你又把 Bitcoin 卖成现金。所以看起来像'哦，我要用 Bitcoin 付你钱'的事，其实是三笔交易、三次不同的转移。而我觉得他所描述的很多这类事情——你怎么能在 Rome 存钱、然后一到 London 就把它取出来——正是这样一种本质：很多时候，看起来像一笔交易的东西，其实是一笔庞大的多环节（multi-leg）交易，可以像乐高积木那样被拆解并以多种方式重新组合。

turns.en: Yeah, which means there are all these little like vulnerabilities and steps that you can end up exploiting. Well, also on the crypto thing, it was interesting to hear that money laundering is predominantly about stable coins.
turns.zh: 是啊，这意味着有所有这些小小的漏洞和步骤，你最终可以加以利用。嗯，另外说到 crypto 那件事，很有意思的是听说洗钱主要关乎稳定币。

turns.en: Yeah, I was surprised.
turns.zh: 是啊，我很惊讶。

turns.en: And that kind of gets back to the seniorage point, which is if you think of stable coins as something that nowadays finances U.S. government debt because a lot of the money goes into U.S. treasuries. then you're back to this idea that, well, maybe people aren't particularly incentivized to crack down on what's essentially an interest-free, well, not in the case of Treasury, but a loan to the U.S.
turns.zh: 这多少又回到了铸币税那个点上，也就是：如果你把稳定币看作如今在资助 U.S. 政府债务的东西——因为很多钱流进了 U.S. 国债（U.S. treasuries）——那你就又回到这个想法：嗯，也许人们并没有特别强的动力去打击这种本质上是一笔无息的——好吧，在 Treasury 的情况下不算无息——但总之是对 U.S. ……的贷款。

turns.en: Government.
turns.zh: 政府。

turns.en: It's also interesting just generally that whenever you're talking about money laundering or crime, you use a metric that is very rarely ever discussed in economics, which is dollar value per unit of spatial volume, right? Because that is a rare metric. But that's what we're talking about. Like if it's like, why is a Rolex a useful vehicle? It's because a high dollar value at a small spatial volume. And so like, what is the $ 200 bill or $ 100 bill on a Rolex and other things have in common? The opposite of get would be like, I don't know, a giant couch or something like that. It's probably like a pretty inefficient way to do it.
turns.zh: 还有一件有意思的事，泛泛地说：每当你谈论洗钱或犯罪时，你都会用到一个在经济学里极少被讨论的度量，也就是单位空间体积的美元价值（dollar value per unit of spatial volume），对吧？因为那是个罕见的度量。但那正是我们在谈论的东西。就像，为什么一块 Rolex 是一种有用的载体？就是因为它在小空间体积里有很高的美元价值。所以，200 美元钞票、或 100 美元钞票跟 Rolex 及其他东西有什么共同点？其反面大概是——我不知道——一张巨大的沙发之类的。那大概是相当低效的做法。
